summary:
Since decades ago, terrain in Maneadero, a town near Ensenada, has begun to experience a salinization effect due to having to use water from sources other than those which nature provides such as rain or rivers.

Local farmers have been struck economically and commonly pay big businesses to asses their farms and deliver crop rotation strategies. Using NASA and external satellite data we focused on empowering experienced and inexperienced farmers into having orbital data with values such as soil health and weather tendencies be humanly interpretable, WITHOUT removing their own decisions. Our app will let people in agriculture visualize their farm and run 3500~ crop rotations in simulations of 30 years to determine optimal strategies.
details:
Inspiration

Centro de Investigación Científica y de Educación Superior de Ensenada, Baja California. (2022, March 25). Aguas subterráneas: entre sobreexplotación y salinidad [Groundwater: Between overexploitation and salinity]. https://www.cicese.edu.mx/cicese3/difusion/getDatosDifusionId/1056 

Since a few years ago, national research institutes such as CICESE and UABC have begun multiple investigations into the soil in Maneadero. The site states that Maneadero aquifers suffer from salinization due to using more water than rainfall provides, bringing up the issue of how the unpredictability of changing weather patterns makes it difficult for inexperienced farmers to learn how to plant. The problem being so close to home made us want to spring into action and come up with a possible solution.

What does Good to Grow do? 

Good to Grow is an app that helps farmers decide what to plant next using NASA data for their own field. It analyses 30 years of local conditions, water flow, and soil erosion risk to create a 3-year crop rotation plan, comparing the farmer´s current approach with alternative options and their tradeoffs, goal by goal. Additionally, an AI assistant helps farmers understand the results by explaining unfamiliar information in simple terms, answering questions and lets farmers discuss their decisions with an agent. Meanwhile, user memory keeps their field information and goals saved from season to season, allowing for more personalized recommendations over time.

How does it work? 

First, the farmer selects their plot on the map. With the help of MapLibre globe visualization we are able to pinpoint the coordinate selected and proceed to gain specific information of what the goals for the rotation of the farmer are: the farmers current plan, what they plant today and what matters most to them (saving water, earning more, building healthier soil, or a mix).  Then the website fetches locally from POWER API:

  • T2M_MAX/T2M_MIN → daily max / min temperature
  • PRECTOTCORR → Precipitation mm/day
  • ALLSKY_SFTC_SW_DWN → Solar Radiation that reaches the ground MJ/m2/day
  • RH2M → Relative humidity at 2m
  • WS2M → Wind Speed at 2m

With these values we are able to calculate the Evapotranspiration of the farm using the following equation:

While this is running, the app has fetched all of the following data:

  • 30 years of daily NASA POWER weather (1995–2024)
  • ISRIC SoilGrids soil
  • NASA SRTM elevation for the land's slope
  • One Landsat image per year since 1995, shown as a time-lapse while the analysis runs

For hardware, an Arduino Nano and a soil moisture sensor detect moisture levels; for this demo, we used a potted basil plant as a simulation for a field. The Arduino is left recording data overnight and into the morning, data which we used to model a differential equation that tells us about the constant “k” for the soil, as well as “t” time; This equation helps farmers compare real on-the-field data with satellite information. Providing clear, measurable, and comparable data.

According to our test, ambient moisture reached a raw ADC value of 573.8; at “t” = 0, the sensor raw ADC unit was 699. The equation resulted as follows:

dm/dt = k(m - 573.8)

After which we applied our initial values as specified before, solving to get a D.E. for moisture according to “t” time in hours:

m(t)  = 128.9 · e^(−0.2192·t) + 573.8 

This data is then displayed directly onto the feed; this helps with calculations regarding water drainage and retention. It is important to note that this is only for the small one and a half day test for a potted basil; this is just for demonstration purposes.

The app proceeds to simulate ~3500 possible 3-year crop rotations against 30 years of the real historical weather and climate data from that exact location by turning weather into water demand: the engine computes daily crop water demand with FAO-56 Penman–Monteith (ET₀), plus frost, heat, and dry-year statistics. The best rotations are shown side by side with the farmer’s current practice, on a 3D model of their own land, so the comparison is concrete and visual. The user has the possibility of auditing the plan with the agent and suggesting, from their own experience, different rotations:

Figure. Main dashboard with agent window open, suggesting different rotations.

Figure. Selection wheel for different personalized plans.

What benefit does it provide?

Our main goal is to turn numerical data that may seem too overwhelming for an average farmer with not much experience in agronomy, but with experience in cultivating  (the intended audience), into simplified and human results that anybody can understand, alongside an AI partner that helps them develop a better critical understanding of how changing parts of the field may change the outcome.

In a broader sense, we would like to see this tool being used to improve the massive water usage in farms, and to regain the economic advantage that Mexico and neighboring countries possess as a farming global power.

Problem solving

Most of the problems we faced came from working with information that was new to us, so we had to learn quickly and find workarounds along the way. To understand the challenge, we researched topics such as evapotranspiration, which became the basis for how our engine estimates crop water use.

One of the first obstacles was that the libraries we used had no Earth snapshots for 2012, because of no usable imagery for that year in NASA's data. The SoilGrids API was also too slow to rely on, so we built a fallback with default soil values and flagged it in the interface whenever it is used. The most complex challenge was making sure our agent never invents data and that its feedback is well-founded. For this, we made it so that the agent can only state figures that come from the engine's tools, so it never estimates or calculates numbers itself. Also, any change to a plan only happens after the farmer taps Allow. 

Hardware development presented various compatibility issues, such as limited sensor data, incompatible values or limited application. A great deal of time was spent making sure the data coming up from the sensors actually mattered, as well as including the possibility of adding a new sensor.

What aspects could we improve if we had more time?

Given more time, we would focus on four key improvements. First, we would integrate NPK (nitrogen, phosphorus, and potassium) sensors into our hardware to gather richer soil data and generate even more accurate recommendations; we would also improve sensor components such that they provide clearer resolution, less noise, and more control. Second, we would field-test the system on local farms to refine our software and strengthen our hardware's durability under real-world conditions, making sure that the hardware checks gather enough resolution to model polished equations determining water evaporation and drainage. Third, we would enhance user security by implementing password-protected authentication. Finally, we would expand our database to support a wider variety of crops. 

Tools used for this project

Languages: TypeScript, C++

Frameworks: Vite & React

Hardware: Arduino Nano, Soil moisture sensor

Libraries: MapLibreGL, Three.js

References: FAO 56, FAO 29, FAO EcoCorp

NOTE: No visual assets or art inside the project was generated by artificial intelligence/super intelligence

Code generation, Agent creation: Claude Opus 5.5
